qs.q: What type of cholinergic receptor is located at synapses between preganglionic and postganglionic autonomic neurons?
qs.e: All autonomic ganglia utilize nicotinic cholinergic receptors for transmission between preganglionic and postganglionic neurons. Muscarinic receptors are typically located at parasympathetic target organs.

qs.q: Which cholinergic receptor is found at synapses between autonomic preganglionic and postganglionic neurons?
qs.e: Preganglionic autonomic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors on postganglionic neurons in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia.

qs.q: Which type of cholinergic receptor is found at synapses between preganglionic and postganglionic neurons of the sympathetic system?
qs.e: The neurotransmitter at the synapse between preganglionic and postganglionic neurons in both the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems is acetylcholine (ACh). This ACh acts on nicotinic receptors on the postganglionic neuron.

faq.a: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors only; nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction remain overstimulated, causing weakness.
faq.q: Why does atropine not improve muscle weakness in organophosphate poisoning?

faq.a: In myasthenia, anticholinesterases improve strength; in cholinergic excess, they worsen symptoms.
faq.q: How can you tell myasthenia gravis from a cholinergic crisis?

faq.a: Excessive sweating, salivation, and pinpoint pupils together (miosis) are classic muscarinic signs.
faq.q: What bedside sign suggests a muscarinic excess?

exam: A 30‑year‑old farmer presents with sweating, vomiting, and bradycardia after pesticide exposure – what is your immediate pharmacologic priority and why? — Administer atropine promptly to block muscarinic effects; consider pralidoxime later to reactivate AChE.

A patient with fluctuating ptosis improves after edrophonium – what does this indicate and what is the next diagnostic step? — Suggests myasthenia gravis; obtain anti‑AChR antibodies or repeat EMG if available.

During surgery you notice unexpected muscle relaxation despite adequate neuromuscular blocker dosing – which receptor problem should you suspect? — Possible pre‑existing nicotinic blockade from chronic organophosphate exposure; check exposure history.
A child with botulism shows descending paralysis – which test is most useful if laboratory facilities are lacking? — Serial bedside forced vital capacity measurements to monitor respiratory decline.

Explain why a patient on a beta‑blocker develops severe bronchospasm after receiving a cholinergic agonist – what receptor interaction is responsible? — Muscarinic M₃ activation causes bronchial smooth‑muscle contraction; beta‑blockade removes opposing β₂ bronchodilation.

In a low‑resource clinic you cannot measure serum cholinesterase – how do you confirm organophosphate poisoning? — Rely on clinical SLUDGE syndrome and rapid response to atropine; document exposure history.

Why are nicotinic receptors at the autonomic ganglia less affected by low‑dose organophosphate poisoning than muscarinic receptors? — Ganglionic nicotinic receptors have higher ACh turnover and are less susceptible to modest AChE inhibition.

A patient on anticholinergic medication develops urinary retention – which receptor subtype is implicated and why? — Muscarinic M₃ receptors in the bladder detrusor muscle are blocked, reducing contraction.
ai.title: Cholinergic Receptors
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Cholinergic receptors mediate acetylcholine actions in the nervous system and at neuromuscular junctions. Understanding their subtypes, signaling, and clinical implications helps diagnose and manage autonomic and neuromuscular disorders, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Key clinical link: drugs that mimic or block ACh affect heart rate, secretions, bronchi, and muscle strength
sections.p: Acetylcholine (ACh) activates two major receptor families: nicotinic (ion‑channel) and muscarinic (G‑protein‑coupled). They are distributed in the CNS, autonomic ganglia, parasympathetic end‑organs, and skeletal muscle.

b: M₂ in heart → slows SA node (negative chronotropy)
M₃ in airway glands → stimulates bronchial secretion
sections.p: Nicotinic receptors (N₁ at neuromuscular junction, N₂ at autonomic ganglia) open ligand‑gated Na⁺/K⁺ channels. Muscarinic receptors (M₁‑M₅) couple to G‑proteins: M₁, M₃, M₅ → Gq → IP₃/DAG ↑ Ca²⁺; M₂, M₄ → Gi → ↓ cAMP.

b: Presynaptic M₂ receptors provide negative feedback
sections.p: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) hydrolyses ACh in synaptic clefts, terminating signalling. Autonomic balance is maintained by reciprocal sympathetic (adrenergic) and parasympathetic (cholinergic) tone.

b: Myasthenia gravis – auto‑antibodies block N₁ receptors → fluctuating weakness
Organophosphate poisoning – AChE inhibition → cholinergic excess (SLUDGE)
Botulism – presynaptic blockade of ACh release → flaccid paralysis
sections.p: Disruption of cholinergic signalling produces a spectrum of clinical syndromes, from muscle weakness to autonomic crisis.

b: SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis) suggests organophosphate toxicity
Ptosis, diplopia worsening with activity → think myasthenia gravis
Bronchospasm with excessive secretions → consider muscarinic over‑activity
sections.p: Recognising cholinergic patterns guides emergency care, chronic disease management, and drug selection, especially where diagnostic tools are limited.

t.b: Does transient improvement in muscle strength confirm myasthenia gravis? – Positive rapid improvement supports diagnosis; negative does not exclude.
Is low activity diagnostic of organophosphate poisoning? – Very low activity confirms exposure; if unavailable, rely on clinical SLUDGE and response to atropine.
When does respiratory failure risk rise in botulism? – FVC < 15 mL/kg signals impending failure; initiate ventilatory support.
